posts.text:
Mercedes sold its Tesla stake for $780 million. that same 4 percent is worth about $56 billion today.

in the clip below Musk explains how Mercedes ended up there. the US government gave Tesla almost $500 million, and he is asked directly whether that loan saved the company. he says no.

what saved it was a $50 million check from Daimler in May 2009. all of Tesla was worth $550 million then.

"they were the only ones. there was no other company, no other entity of any kind from which we could get investments."

Tesla repaid the government's $500 million with interest and a prepayment penalty, ten years early. he sent a thank you note with it.

"i don't like having a lot of debt. the taxpayers supported Tesla, we ought to repay them as soon as we can."

Mercedes turned $50 million into $780 million and walked away in 2014.

so was that a great investment - or the most expensive mistake in car industry history?

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
I want to expand on this, because for BioWare's original games:

I was the target demographic. 

Baldur's Gate, NWN, KOTOR, ME, DAO were all games that managed to target in my soul what I wanted from a game.

And one by one they killed each of them. Not with a bang, but with the steady decay of the core mechanics and plots.

Well except for KOTOR. That one they just set on fire on the way out, and left modders to pick up the pieces.

Eventually they would release a game, and I'd look at it, think back on what was, and say...

"No. I don't think I will buy that."

Literally all they had to do is hit the rewind button and say "You know that thing that made money that gamers wanted? Let's make that!"

They refused.

quote.author: TheCaptainEli
quote.name: Captain Eli
quote.text:
In September 2014, Elon stood under a tent on an almost empty beach at the very tip of South Texas, waves crashing just over the dunes, and broke ground on a launch site.

In May 2025, he stood in front of a crowd at that same corner of Texas and said it plainly: "not that long ago, there was basically nothing here."

Now it's a city. Literally. On May 3, 2025, Starbase voted to incorporate, 212 to 6. In Elon's words, "the first new city made in America in I think quite a few decades." I love the "I think." Even his victory laps come with error bars.

What gets me is how it got there. One of the first things to fly was Starhopper, a stubby steel tank on legs that he calls "the original sort of Mad Max rocket." In August 2019 it hopped 150 meters. Then came prototypes that flew, flipped and sometimes exploded in full public view, right next to a public highway.

That's his pattern. Pick the thing everyone says is impossible, build it in the open, break it, learn, build the next one, and keep going until the laughing stops. "In the space of about five or six years... we've built a small city... and a gigantic rocket factory for a gigantic rocket."

Then in October 2024 the rocket came home and the launch tower caught it. His reaction: "it's really mind-blowing that the SpaceX team has been able to catch the largest flying object ever made multiple times."

My favorite detail? You can just go and look. Anyone interested in seeing the largest flying object on Earth "can come here anytime they want and just drive down the public highway and see it." Name another place where you can watch the future get welded together from your car window.

Why does a sandbar in Texas matter to me, thousands of kilometers away? Because it proves you don't need permission to build the future. You need a team, a beach, and the stubbornness to stay on it. The mission hasn't changed since the groundbreaking: "to take humanity and civilization and life as we know it to another planet for the first time in the 4 and a half billion year history of Earth."

And the line I keep coming back to: "we can be out there among the stars making science fiction no longer fiction."

From empty dunes to a city that builds Mars ships. I made a short film about it.
